content.title: Renewables are Reshaping the Global South
content.intro: M5: Derisking Renewable Energy Investment (DREI) | Chapter 1 | Lesson 1

content.text: Lesson 1 Overview

Increasing the share of renewable energy in the electricity production mix is one of the objectives within the energy transition, that was contextualised in Module 3. Renewable energy’s wider implementation is needed to fight climate change, increase energy security and promote economic and social development.
This objective is reflected in the Sustainable Development Goals (SDGs), especially SDG 7 – Universal Access to sustainable and modern energy, SDG 13 – Climate Action, and SDG 1 – End poverty.
SDGs 1 and 7 reflect especially the needs for new renewable energy capacity in developing countries, where the gaps in electricity access create barriers to socio-economic development and increase environmental and health impacts due to the use of fossil fuels or low-quality biomass to meet basic energy needs of vulnerable populations.

Renewable energy capacity may be implemented in the form of utility-scale, grid connected projects, that increase the availability of electricity for consumers on the main electricity grids, allow the connection of new consumers and reduce the dependency on imported fuels where a large part of the electricity produced is imported or produced by thermal power plants.
It can also be implemented in the form of decentralised projects, that consist in small-scale generation that is located closer to its consumers and that may be integrated in the grid or implemented independently (off-grid). Decentralised (or distributed) systems include mini-grids powered by diesel, solar PV/batteries or other renewable energy sources, solar home systems 💬️ and other standalone systems both powered using Solar PV/batteries to increase electricity access in remote areas, or Solar PV/battery powered mini-grids and solar PV (in some cases combined with batteries) rooftops that complement grid electricity supply where it is unreliable.

content.title: A: Utility-scale renewable energy investment trends – focus on wind and solar PV

content.body: Renewable energy technologies for electricity production include wind power, solar photovoltaic (PV), concentrated solar power, hydropower, biomass/biogas, marine and geothermal energy.
Hydropower was the first renewable energy source that was used at scale to produce electricity both at utility-scale and small-scale and can be considered a mature technology.
Wind and solar PV have emerged since the beginning of the century and are expected to both have larger installed capacities than hydropower by 2030, according to IEA’s forecast.
Asia, driven mostly by China, since 2015 is responsible for a large share of the capacity of both technologies, while Africa and Latin America represent a very small share of the global capacity.

Even within developing countries, the solar PV capacity is not evenly distributed. China has 74% of Asia’s solar capacity, Brazil has 62% of solar capacity in Latin America, while Mexico has 14% and Chile has 13%.

In Africa, most of the grid-connected solar capacity was implemented in South Africa (6665 MW, 46,5% of Africa total), while 17,6% is in Egypt, 6,4% in Morocco and 5,3% in Tunisia. Only a few countries in Sub-Saharan Africa have more than 150 MW of solar capacity: Angola, Kenya, Senegal, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Namibia and Zambia.

A similar trend is observed for wind power: China concentrates 85% of wind power capacity in Asia while in Latin America, Brazil has 60% of the wind power capacity (33 GW), Mexico has 13%, Chile 9% and Argentina 8%.

16 countries in Africa have installed wind power capacity, most of it in South Africa (37% of capacity), Egypt (24%) and Morocco (23%). Kenya, Ethiopia and Tunisia can be mentioned, with respectively 5%, 4% and 3% of African wind capacity.

In Africa, most of the grid-connected solar capacity was implemented in South Africa (6665 MW, 46,5% of Africa total), while 17,6% is in Egypt, 6,4% in Morocco and 5,3% in Tunisia. Only a few countries in Sub-Saharan Africa have more than 150 MW of solar capacity: Angola, Kenya, Senegal, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Namibia and Zambia.
Do you know of utility-scale wind or solar photovoltaic projects implemented in your country? What is their installed capacity, who implemented, financed them?

content.text: Leading countries in Africa, Asia, Latin America and policies / programs that led to this result:

IRENA has estimated Sub-Saharan Africa’s solar technical potential at almost 5000 GW, and wind technical potential at 237 GW. Mauritania, Niger, Mali, Chad, Ethiopia and Namibia present the largest potential.

However, the exploration of this potential depends on support from governments through adequate policies and regulations, subsidies or other financial support, supported by coherent energy planning, integrated within a wider sustainable development planning process.

Indeed, wind and solar energy 💬️ technologies were until recently more expensive than traditional energy sources, and continue to face barriers that affect their economic and technical viability in developing countries.

content.title: China
content.body:
IEA expects China’s renewable energy capacity, in 2024 consisting of 887 GW of solar and 520 GW of wind capacity, to expand some 3 200 GW between 2024 and 2030, solar PV accounting for 80% of this increase.
While China’s wind and solar PV generation capacity growth until 2020 was fostered by favourable Feed-in tariffs (FIT), since 2021, wind and solar PV plants can benefit from 15- to 20-year power purchase agreements (PPA) at set electricity prices.
Although FIT guaranteed that all the electricity produced by the plants would be remunerated at an advantageous price, the power purchase contracts limit the volume of electricity remunerated, and the prices tend to be lower than the FIT, but they still provide a guarantee of stable and predictable revenue flow for enough time to secure investors.

content.title: India
content.body:
India’s energy mix constitutes 97 GW of solar PV capacity, among which 3 GW off-grid, over 70% of new renewable energy generation capacity will be solar PV, utility-scale projects representing two-thirds of this growth, fuelled by competitive auctions that contracted 33 GW of capacity in the first half of 2024.
40% of the new capacity was awarded to hybrid systems, which combine PV, wind and storage to reduce generation variability and facilitate system integration.

content.title: Latin America
content.body:
In Latin America, wind and solar PV capacity has increased following different drivers. Competitive auctions in Brazil, Mexico and Argentina have originally driven the expansion of wind generation and guaranteed competitive prices for the utilities. However, the procured volumes have declined in recent years, and in some cases policy changes have led to discontinued public procurement.
Bilateral agreements, where industrial customers are contracting large amounts of renewable capacity to meet corporate decarbonisation goals, have on the other hand increased in these countries thanks to the accumulated national experience fostered by the auctions.

content.title: South Africa
content.body:
South Africa has held competitive auctions for wind and solar utility-scale projects since 2011 and has since contracted a total of close to 15 GW, of the 30 GW projected in its Integrated Resource Plan (IRP). Through these auctions, bidders are invited to present their wind and solar PV power plants projects, demonstrating technical and environmental viability, as well as minimum participation of national investors, among them Black and local communities. Among the selected bidders, the lowest selling prices for electricity are selected and awarded 20-year PPAs with the public utility.
These auctions have attracted a large number of developers and investors, guaranteed competitive prices and paved the way for the implantation of local components manufacturers in the country.
What programs in your country are implemented to support the development of wind and solar energy? How did they evolve over time?

content.text:
Renewable electricity generation, including hydropower and other renewables (mostly bioenergy, concentrated solar power 💬️ and geothermal energy) is forecast by the International Energy Agency (IEA) to reach globally 17 000 TWh by 2030, equivalent to 46% of global electricity generation. It is almost 90% more than was observed in 2023. Wind and solar PV are expected to account for 30% of global electricity generation.

Some other forecast tendencies: renewables-based electricity generation will overtake coal-fired by 2025, while solar and wind will overtake nuclear by 2026. Solar PV will surpass wind in 2027 and hydropower in 2030, while wind will surpass hydropower by 2030.
Trends and expectations for the future, main barriers to the expansion of utility-scale wind and solar PV power generation in developing countries.
Focus on Sub-Saharan Africa

The IEA forecasts almost 90 GW of new renewable capacity for sub-Saharan Africa between 2024 and 2030, over 2,5 times the region’s current installed capacity. Solar PV and wind represent nearly 80% of new capacity in the region.

South Africa should be responsible for installing nearly 40% of the region’s new capacity, mainly through its auctions program for utility-scale renewables and distributed solar PV installations, though wind capacity contracted through the auctions is declining due to grid constraints.

New markets are also expected to play a role in solar PV and wind expansion. Nigeria and Kenya combined are expected to be responsible for over 25% of new solar PV capacity in Sub-Saharan Africa.

In Nigeria, 7,5 GW of new distributed solar PV are estimated due to the phaseout of fossil fuel subsidies and frequent blackouts. In Kenya, a Feed-In Tariff program and distributed installations should lead to the addition of over 1,3 GW of new capacity.

Outside of South Africa, policy uncertainty and the lack of long-term planning for wind power development are observed. New projects are mostly backed by national utilities, aid agencies or development banks and face several barriers.

content.title: B: Decentralized renewable electricity generation trends

content.text: Decentralized electricity generation –concept, advantages and focus on renewable energy-based technologies

Decentralised electricity generation technologies differ from utility-scale as they are smaller systems implemented closer to consumers. These systems can be connected to the main grid, through small systems such as rooftop solar PV and wind systems or “undergrid” mini-grids, or independent from the main grid, in the case of the “off-grid” systems.

“There is no viable path to Sustainable Development Goal target 7.1—that is, to ensure universal access to affordable, reliable, and modern energy services—without accelerated deployment of decentralized solutions. But current investment flows fall far short of what is required for the sector to achieve its potential”.
ESMAP, Tracking SDG 7, The Energy market report, 2024.

Off-grid systems include mini-grids, Solar Home Systems, standalone systems which provide energy services for water pumping, cooling, or other productive uses, and solar lamps.
Originally powered primarily by diesel generators, decentralised electricity generation sources are transitioning to hybrid or purely solar PV, wind, biomass 💬️ and small hydropower, often combined with batteries to ensure stable electricity supply (ESMAP, 2023).

The total installed renewable off-grid electricity generation capacity in 2024 globally was according to IRENA statistics 14,7 GW of which 7 GW solar, 5,3 GW biomass-based, 1,6 GW hydropower and 0,2 GW wind.
Among the 7 GW of solar PV, mini-grids accounted for 724 MW, SHS for 425 MW, solar lanterns for 68 MW, solar pumps for 2,5 GW, solar cookers for 77 MW, public lighting systems for 110 MW, while various industrial, agricultural, and unspecified uses accounted for almost 2,4 GW.
Mini - Grids

A mini-grid is an independent system constituted of small-scale electricity generators and possibly electricity storage, connected to a distribution network and delivering electricity to a limited number of consumers – from a dozen to a few thousand.

The generation capacity of mini-grids varies from a few kW (therefore denominated “nano-grid” or “micro-grid”), to a few MW (sometimes denominated "metro-grid”).

Although historically, most mini-grids were diesel-based, and some small hydropower-based and biomass-based mini-grids were implemented early, the current dominant models for mini-grid are hybrid diesel-solar PV, and solar PV with batteries.

According to ESMAP, in 2022, an estimated 21 500 mini-grids, among which half solar PV-powered, were serving 48 million people. Half of those were solar or solar-diesel hybrids, 35% hydropower, 10% fossil-fuels and 5% wind or fuel cells-powered.

In 2023, 5,8 million people were connected to solar mini-grids of a total capacity of close to 724 MW, according to IRENA statistics. 2,57 million of these consumers were in Africa, while 3,09 million were in Asia an 0,14 million in Latin America.
Definition – Energy Tiers

ESMAP’s database in 2022 counted with some 30 000 planned mini-grids, among them 19 000 in South Asia (mostly India) and 9000 in Africa. Nigeria, Tanzania and Senegal are the 3 countries with the most planned mini-grids in Africa. Most of these new planned mini-grids are either solar PV-batteries or solar PV-diesel hybrid mini-grids.

ESMAP’s least-cost modelling to achieve SDG 7 indicates that mini-grids are the least-cost electrification solution for up to 429,5 million people who still lack access to electricity, most of them in Sub-Saharan Africa.least-cost modelling to achieve SDG 7 indicates that mini-grids are the least-cost electrification solution for up to 429,5 million people who still lack access to electricity, most of them in Sub-Saharan Africa.

content.body: Tier 1. This is the lowest level, and provides energy for an average annual consumption of 22 kWh per household. In concrete terms, this is barely enough to switch on a few lightbulbs, charge a phone or turn on a radio;

Tier 2. This covers ten times the consumption of level 1, providing for an annual use of 224 kWh per household. It enables the operation of general lighting, air circulation systems and even a television;

Tier 3. At this level, we find the first domestic appliances, such as a washing machine, and some kitchen appliances, like a blender. The amount of available energy allows a maximum consumption of 696 kWh;

Tier 4. You need to be at the fourth level to have a fridge or hot water. It means having a capacity of around 1,800 kWh per year, an energy level which many developing countries cannot access. Yet no one in western countries would consider a dwelling to be habitable without a fridge or hot water.

Tier 5. At the fifth level, families have enough electricity to enjoy general lighting and continuous use of high-power domestic appliances such as refrigeration, air conditioning and possibly a kitchen.

content.text:
Mini-grids can be isolated, or “off-grid”, when located far from the main grid and used as a rural electrification solution. Some mini-grids are installed in localities where the main grid already exists, but does not deliver a satisfactory service. They are denominated “undergrid mini-grids” and can operate both connected to the main grid, exchanging electricity with the main grid or complementing the electricity supply, or independently, to guarantee the local electricity supply when the main grid fails.
Some mini-grids have the capacity to supply electricity for up to 24 hours a day and support high loads, therefore allowing productive uses of electricity and rural industrialisation.
Solar lanterns and Solar Home Systems (SHS)

Solar lanterns, or Pico solar systems, are PV-powered devices that provide mostly lighting, and in some cases light electricity applications such as phone and loudspeakers charging. Their capacities vary between 1 and 10 Wp.

Solar Home Systems are individual systems composed of solar PV modules with a battery, an inverter and cables that deliver electricity through plugs to appliances such as TV, fans, small fridges, phone charging and lamps. They are projected to supply electricity to households, small businesses and community services in isolated areas, although they also have been adopted in regions where the main grid supply is unreliable. Their capacity usually varies from a few Watts up to 1 kW.

Their capacities can be as high as 2 kW and they typically consist of specific energy services such as such as water pumps, solar-powered fridges and freezers, agricultural mills, and others.

India was in 2023 the country with the largest total solar water pumping capacity, at 1252 MW mostly for agricultural use (representing almost one million water pumps), followed by Bangladesh with 49 MW and Nepal with 4,3 MW.

These systems are usually deployed through international development programs and with government subsidies, motivated by reduction of greenhouse gases emissions by replacing diesel-powered appliances and income generation opportunities for remote rural populations. Solar powered water pump especially contributes to improving the quality of life of rural populations, saving time previously used to fetch water and improving agricultural productivity and reducing vulnerability to droughts.
Standalone Systems

Solar PV rooftops are the main grid-connected decentralized electricity generation technology. They account for 40% of global solar PV capacity, and one third of them (close to 190 GW) are residential installations, at a number estimated at 25 million worldwide. IEA expects that residential installations will reach 100 million by 2030.

Supportive policies in developed countries such as Germany, the USA, Italy, the Netherlands and Japan have contributed to high penetration rates. Among developing countries, India, China and Brazil also have developed large capacities. Supportive policies include net billing and surplus feed-in tariff for prosumers.
Grid-connected solar rooftop PV
Main barriers to the development of decentralized electricity generation technologies

The main challenge to the development of decentralized renewable energy-powered electricity generation technologies is their cost. Although the costs of solar PV and batteries technologies have significantly decreased in the last 20 years, many of the potential users are low and middle-income populations from rural areas and who cannot afford the upfront costs of the systems, or cost-reflective electricity tariffs in the case of mini-grids. takeaways.title: Global Shift: Renewables Growing in Capacity and Share
takeaways.description: Increasing electricity demand and the need to reduce fossil-fuel generation in developing countries is increasing the need for renewable energy both in capacity and share of the total electricity production. 1865 GW of solar PV capacity and 1133 GW of wind capacity are estimated to be installed globally. Solar and wind power together are expected to supply 30% of global electricity demand by 2030.

takeaways.title: Asia Dominates Global Solar and Wind Capacity; Africa Holds a Small Share
takeaways.description: While Asia, led by China, accounts for 67% of global solar capacity and 53% of wind power capacity, only 0,8% of capacities from both sources are located in Africa. A significant portion of the 0.8 % is concentrated in South Africa and in North African countries. Large government-led procurement programs are responsible for the large capacities installed in China and other leading countries, while others, including Sub-Saharan African countries lack policies and capacity to foster the needed investment, creating favourable environments and reducing risk for investors.

takeaways.title: Decentralized Renewables Expanding Energy Access in Africa and Asia
takeaways.description: Decentralized renewable energy-based electricity generation technologies include mostly grid-connected rooftop solar systems, renewable energy-based mini-grids and Solar Home Systems. 45 million people, mostly in Africa and Asia, have access to electricity through renewable energy-powered mini-grids and Solar Home Systems, while a few million of solar-powered water pumps are estimated to have been installed worldwide, mostly in India.
